reference.source: Hazzard's Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology / palliative care guidelines
clinicalPearls: Orthostatic hypotension is conventionally defined as a sustained fall in systolic blood pressure of at least 20 mmHg, or diastolic of at least 10 mmHg, within three minutes of standing
Symptoms include light-headedness, dizziness, visual dimming, weakness, and falls on standing, but many older adults are asymptomatic
Measure blood pressure supine and then after standing, ideally at one and three minutes, to detect both early and delayed drops
Medications are among the commonest and most reversible causes, including antihypertensives, diuretics, nitrates, alpha-blockers, and drugs with anticholinergic or vasodilating effects
Volume depletion from dehydration, bleeding, or diuretics should always be considered and corrected
Neurogenic causes include diabetic and other autonomic neuropathies and neurodegenerative disorders such as Parkinson disease and related synucleinopathies
Non-drug management comes first: gradual position change, adequate fluid and salt intake where appropriate, compression garments, avoiding large meals and alcohol, and reviewing culprit drugs
A large post-prandial blood pressure fall is a related phenomenon in older adults and can also precipitate falls and syncope
reference.pathophysiology: On standing, gravity shifts blood to the lower body, and normally baroreceptor-mediated reflex increases in heart rate and vascular tone maintain cerebral perfusion. Ageing blunts baroreflex sensitivity and reduces cardiac and vascular compensatory responses. Orthostatic hypotension develops when these mechanisms fail, either because of impaired autonomic reflexes (neurogenic causes) or because of reduced circulating volume or vasodilating and blood-pressure-lowering drugs (non-neurogenic causes). The resulting transient cerebral hypoperfusion produces symptoms and predisposes to falls and syncope.
additionalDifferentials: Cardiac arrhythmia or structural heart disease causing syncope
additionalInvestigations: Lying and standing blood pressure measurements at one and three minutes
Medication review to identify contributing agents
Assessment of hydration status and relevant bloods including electrolytes and haemoglobin
ECG and cardiac evaluation when arrhythmia or structural disease is suspected
Evaluation for autonomic neuropathy or neurodegenerative disease when a neurogenic cause is likely
redFlags: Syncope resulting in injury or occurring without warning
Orthostatic drop accompanied by chest pain, palpitations, or signs of cardiac disease
Evidence of significant volume loss such as gastrointestinal bleeding
Recurrent falls attributable to postural drops
Severe, treatment-resistant orthostatic hypotension suggesting advanced autonomic failure
reference.prognosis: Orthostatic hypotension is common in older adults and is associated with falls, syncope, reduced quality of life, and higher cardiovascular and overall mortality. Many cases improve substantially once contributing medications are withdrawn, volume is restored, and non-pharmacological measures are applied, though neurogenic forms can be chronic and challenging.
pitfalls: Measuring standing blood pressure only once and missing delayed orthostatic drops
Overlooking medications as the reversible cause
Failing to consider volume depletion or occult bleeding
Aggressively treating supine hypertension in ways that worsen orthostatic symptoms
Not recognising post-prandial hypotension as a distinct contributor to falls
management: Review and rationalise contributing drugs — antihypertensives, diuretics, nitrates, alpha-blockers and agents with vasodilating or anticholinergic effects — and correct volume depletion
Non-pharmacological measures first: liberalising salt and fluid intake, graduated compression garments or an abdominal binder, physical counter-manoeuvres, slow staged rising and head-up sleeping
Pharmacological therapy when non-drug measures fail, using a volume expander such as fludrocortisone or a pressor such as midodrine or droxidopa, particularly in neurogenic causes
Identify and treat the underlying cause, including diabetic or other autonomic neuropathy and neurodegenerative synucleinopathies such as Parkinson disease
Monitor for and avoid provoking supine hypertension, balancing daytime symptom control against nocturnal blood pressure
Falls-prevention assessment and patient education on recognising and aborting presyncopal symptoms
Referral to geriatric, cardiology or autonomic specialist services for refractory or neurogenic disease
